sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No. The lead picture (about 60–829 × 130–437 px) is a flat brick-red field with a pale pink circle cut off at its bottom edge. The caption below it says "Rose arch / Climbing roses over the east gate", but the picture shows no roses, no arch and no gate. The same is true of all six tiles. "Herb bed" (843–1220 × 130–274), "Pond edge", "Bean rows", "Glasshouse" and "Orchard path" are each one solid colour with the same half-circle. This is a gallery of a garden show, so the pictures are the content. As it stands, a viewer gets six coloured swatches and has to take every caption on trust. Nothing on the page shows them a garden or makes them want to visit one. Either the photos failed to load or these are placeholder art left in. If they are placeholders, this is a defect; if the capture missed the photos, the page may be fine once real photos load. The direction of the fix: put a real photograph of each exhibit in each tile, and make the "Rose arch" lead picture actually show the arch, since it carries the page. Marked defect. The catalog entry ("Visual and headline work together") has no approved source, so this rests on common sense. Weight: major.
2. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No. The pale half-circle repeats in the centre of every tile, at about 290–598 px wide on the lead tile and about 150 px on the small ones. It carries no information and doesn't tell one exhibit from another; only the background colour changes. If it is meant as decoration rather than a stand-in for photos, remove it. If it stands in for photos, it goes when finding 1 is fixed. This is part of the same problem as finding 1. Marked defect (common sense; Nielsen heuristic 8, aesthetic and minimalist design). Weight: minor on its own.

**What's working.**
- **Consistent cards.** The five small cards repeat one pattern: picture, then a bold name (about 14 px), then a grey one-line description. "Rose arch" is clearly a deliberate feature, with a bigger picture, a heading of about 36 px and a larger description. The page reads as one system with one lead item, not a collage.
- **Specific headings.** Every heading names its exhibit plainly ("Pond edge", "Bean rows"), and each description adds something concrete ("Reeds and water lilies.", "Tomatoes in late July."). A visitor knows exactly what each tile is meant to show.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether real photos are meant to load into these tiles. Check the live page with a slow network and with images blocked.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; every element does a job)

Two notes on how I ran this:
- Bash was denied in this session, so I couldn't run `scripts/crop.mjs` or `scripts/entries.mjs`. The image is one screen, so I judged it from the whole image. For the entries I read part of `references/art-direction.md` directly.
- A small taste point with no checklist line behind it: "Garden show gallery" doesn't say which show or which year.

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the large red "Rose arch" block, which is the biggest and most saturated shape. The black "Garden show gallery" title above it also pulls, but the two support each other: the title says what the page is, and the feature is the first thing in it. After that the eye moves to the "Rose arch" label, then the right column, then the bottom row. It reads as a small gallery of garden-show photos with one featured item, and it feels calm and tidy. The pictures look like placeholders, but that is outside this section.

Job (assumed): a web gallery page where visitors browse photos from a garden show, with one exhibit featured.

Crops: Bash was refused, so I worked from the whole image. It is about 1280×800, one screen, so it would not have been cropped anyway.

- One element dominates: **yes.** The Rose arch tile (about 60–830 × 130–437 px) is about four times the area of any other tile and has the strongest color.
- Distinct text levels: **yes.** I see five sizes: page title (~64 px), feature heading (~40 px), feature caption (~18 px), tile titles (~14 px bold), tile captions (~13 px gray). The only close pair is the last two, and they are separated by weight and color, which is the right tool there.
- Headings differ by more than size: **yes.** All headings are bold near-black, and captions are regular gray.

No line answered no or unsure, so there were no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The featured tile makes a clear focal point.** "Rose arch" (about 60–830 × 130–437 px) gets about four times the area of the other tiles, the strongest color, and its own ~40 px heading. A visitor knows straight away which exhibit is the feature and where to start. The five smaller tiles are all the same size, so after the feature they read as one even set to browse. Keep that size gap if tiles are added.
- **The small text levels are separated by weight and color, not size.** The tile titles (~14 px bold, near-black) and captions (~13 px regular, gray) are almost the same size but still read as two levels. That keeps the type scale small (title, feature heading, feature caption, tile title, caption) without the sizes colliding.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?"**
   - **Where:** The "Rose arch" caption sits about 15 px below its image (image bottom ≈ y 437, caption ≈ y 450–515). It sits about the same distance above the bottom row (Bean rows / Glasshouse at y 530). Every small caption does the same on a tighter scale. "Herb bed" starts about 9 px under its image (y 274), and its second line ends about 15 px above the next tile (y 330). The same holds for Pond edge.
   - **What the viewer meets:** "Rose arch" is the second-largest text on the page, and it sits in a gap shared equally by two blocks. So it reads for a moment as a section heading over the bottom row ("Rose arch" over Bean rows and Glasshouse), not as the hero's caption. In the right column, captions and tiles run together as one even stack. You can work out which caption goes with which picture, but nothing settles it at a glance.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II, on grouping by location (Wertheimer's proximity rule). A label must sit clearly nearer its own field than the next one, and near-equal gaps erase the groups.
   - **Fix:** Pull each caption tight under its own picture and open the gap between one tile-plus-caption and the next. The between-group gap should clearly exceed the within-group gap, roughly double. For the hero, that means more space above the bottom row than between the red image and "Rose arch".
   - **Type and weight:** Defect. Major for the hero caption, because it is the most prominent label in the gallery. The same problem in the small captions is minor.

**What's working.**
- **The grid is strict and readable.** It has three equal columns of about 377 px (x 60–437, 451–828, 843–1220) with one fixed 14 px gutter, and the hero spans exactly two of them. The right-column tiles repeat on a steady 200 px row step. Every edge comes from the same column lines, so the page looks built rather than placed by eye.
- **The hero breaks the grid decisively.** It ends at y 437, a clear 37 px off the right tiles' edge at y 474, so the difference reads as a choice and not a miss. Its 2:1 scale against the small tiles gives the page a clear first stop.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the layout holds its column and row alignment when the screen width changes. That matters because the hero's caption height and the right-column stack only line up at the bottom at this width. Also, Bash was denied, so I couldn't make crops. All pixel positions are by eye from the whole image (about 1280×800).

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (space inside each group clearly smaller than space between groups).

I found nothing wrong in the Text section: all 30 lines pass. I couldn't run the crop script because the shell was denied, so I judged everything from the whole image (about one screen, 1280×800).

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

The only line I hesitated on was caption size. The grey descriptions under the five small tiles ("Thyme, sage and chives." at about y 308, "Reeds and water lilies." at about y 508, and the three at about y 708) look about 12 px. The guideline's test is whether the letters can be told apart at the image's size, and they can, so that line is a yes. If someone measures them and they come in under 12 px, raise them to 13–14 px, which would also bring them closer to the bold labels above. I couldn't confirm the size without a crop or a measured facts file.

**What's working.**
- **The type plan is simple and clear.** There is one sans family with a few distinct levels:
  - the tightly spaced bold title, "Garden show gallery";
  - a large bold heading with an 18 px-ish regular line for the featured "Rose arch";
  - a small bold label with a smaller grey description for each of the other five tiles.

  The levels are told apart by size, weight and colour rather than by sizes only a few pixels apart. That keeps the featured tile clearly above the rest and lets the five small tiles read as equals.
- **The large type is spaced tighter than the text.** The 64 px-ish title and the "Rose arch" heading are set tight, so they hold together as single shapes and don't look like enlarged body text.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The caption size in CSS px, and whether it stays readable at mobile widths when the tiles reflow.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece use a small palette, about one neutral range and one or two hues besides the status colors?** and **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?**: These two lines are one finding.
   - **Where:** The six picture tiles each use a different strong hue at about the same saturation: brick red (Rose arch, about 60,130 to 829,437), sage green (Herb bed), steel blue (Pond edge), ochre (Bean rows), mustard (Glasshouse) and purple (Orchard path). Each has a paler disc of the same hue. Together they cover roughly half the canvas, and the rest is white with dark gray type.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The page looks like a box of paint chips rather than a garden show. Size makes the red hero lead, but the mustard and purple tiles pull just as hard for their area, so the eye jumps between colors instead of moving across the gallery. There is no color system tying the tiles to each other or to the show.
   - **Why:** This is the triadic/tetradic failure where several vivid hues of equal strength fight with no dominant hue (Itten, *The Art of Color*, color chords). It is also a set of one-off hues with no defined palette (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*, "Define your shades").
   - **What would make it fine:** The tiles sit exactly where the photos go, and the flat disc-on-color motif looks like placeholder art. If real photos of the gardens replace them, this is not a finding, because photos are outside the palette count. In that case, check those photos instead.
   - **Fix direction, if the blocks are final:** Pick one lead color for the hero, which the red already is. Turn the other tiles into light tints or muted shades of one or two related hues, so the hero is the only full-strength block.
   - **Kind:** Defect. **Weight:** major if the blocks are final art, none if they are placeholders.

**What's working.**
- **Value carries the structure.** In grayscale it still reads as a near-black title, mid-gray blocks on white, and dark captions, so the layout holds without hue.
- **Warm color sits on the focus.** The only warm-red tile is also the largest, so color and size agree on where to start (Itten, warm-cool contrast). The white gutters keep neighboring hues from touching, so no edges vibrate.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the colored tiles are final art, placeholder art, or images that failed to load. Check the live page or the image sources. This decides whether finding 1 stands.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 7 yes, 2 no (small palette; saturated color kept to a small share).

sections.report:
**Section.** Pictures: applies. There are six picture tiles: one hero and five thumbnails.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box? No.**
   - **Where:** All six picture slots are generic placeholders. Each is a flat colour field with a pale, lighter-tint circle cut off by the bottom edge:
     - Rose arch: about x 60–829, y 130–437.
     - Herb bed: about 843–1220 × 130–274.
     - Pond edge: about 843–1220 × 330–474.
     - Bean rows: about 60–437 × 530–674.
     - Glasshouse: about 451–829 × 530–674.
     - Orchard path: about 843–1220 × 530–674.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The page is called "Garden show gallery", and its whole job is to show the garden. The viewer sees no roses, herbs, pond, beans, tomatoes or trees, only colour swatches. The captions ("Climbing roses over the east gate", "Reeds and water lilies") describe pictures that aren't there, so the gallery gives the viewer nothing to look at. The colours suggest the subject (red for roses, green for herbs, blue for the pond), but a hint isn't a picture.
   - **Why:** There's no catalogue entry for this, so it's a common-sense judgement: a gallery whose images show nothing fails at its main job.
   - **What would make it fine:** The tiles are stand-ins in a mock-up and will be swapped for real photos before review. If they are placeholder art that should have loaded, check that in a live browser.
   - **Fix direction:** Put a real photograph of each named subject in each slot. Give the hero the strongest image, because its size already makes it the focal point.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.

**What's working.** The picture slots are clearly set up to hold a consistent set:
- **One shape for the set.** All five thumbnails share one aspect ratio and size, and the hero is a clear step up. Real photos will drop into a steady rhythm.
- **One treatment for every tile.** Each has a flat field, a centred circle and the same bottom crop. That one consistent style is the right instinct for a photo set (one crop style and one subject distance) once real images go in.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content).
